pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Mary Anning, Fossil Hunter (ages 7–9): know who Mary Anning was — a pioneering fossil hunter from Lyme Regis on England's south coast who, in the early 1800s, found ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons and helped scientists realise that extinct creatures once lived on Earth.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1/KS2 History (significant individuals who contributed to national/international achievements; Anning is a named exemplar) and science 'working scientifically'/scientists-and-their-work; strong local-heritage relevance.
• Standards — US (NGSS/NGSS-adjacent): supports the 'science is done by diverse people' framing and the fossil-evidence strand (3-LS4-1); a biography that humanises palaeontology.
• Operational details — Cover three things: (1) WHO/WHEN/WHERE — Lyme Regis, early 1800s, hunted fossils in the cliffs (dangerous work, landslides); (2) WHAT — famous finds including the first correctly identified ichthyosaur (found as a child with her brother) and the first complete plesiosaur, plus a pterosaur and important coprolite work; (3) WHY IT MATTERS — her fossils were key evidence that whole kinds of animals had gone EXTINCT, at a time when that idea was new; and she was a working-class woman who was often not credited and was barred from the (all-male) Geological Society. This last point makes her a natural doorway to 'who gets to do science / who gets remembered'. Note her creatures were marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): says Mary Anning found fossils by the sea in England long ago. Tier B (~8): names a find (ichthyosaur or plesiosaur) and that she lived in the early 1800s. Tier C (~9): explains her work helped prove extinction and that she was often not credited because she was a poor woman.
bestPractices: Tell it as a STORY with a real person's obstacles (poverty, danger, being overlooked as a woman) — narrative and stakes make a biography stick.
Anchor to place: the Lyme Regis cliffs (Jurassic Coast) and the hazardous cliff-fall hunting that killed her dog Tray and nearly her.
Foreground the significance — her fossils were evidence for extinction when that idea was radical — so children see WHY she matters, not just what she found.
Address credit/gender honestly at an age-appropriate level: her discoveries were often published by men without naming her; she couldn't join the Geological Society.
Clarify the classification point: ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs (links to Real vs Fiction).
keyRepresentations: A Lyme Regis cliff scene with Anning hunting fossils and her key finds labelled (ichthyosaur, plesiosaur).
A simple timeline of her life and discoveries in the early 1800s.
'What her fossils proved': a before/after on the idea of extinction.
A 'credit then vs now' contrast: unnamed in old papers → celebrated today.
commonMisconceptions: 'Mary Anning found dinosaurs' — her famous finds (ichthyosaur, plesiosaur) were marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Fossil hunting was a safe hobby' — she worked dangerous, crumbling sea cliffs and sold fossils to survive.
'She was a trained, wealthy scientist' — she was a self-taught working-class woman, largely outside the formal scientific establishment.
'She was always famous and credited' — much of her work was published by men without acknowledging her; recognition came largely later.
'Her finds didn't change science' — they were crucial evidence that extinction was real.

learn.summary: Learners aged 7–9 come to know Mary Anning (1799–1847) of Lyme Regis as a self-taught, working-class fossil hunter who found important marine-reptile skeletons in the early 1800s, understand why those finds mattered as evidence for extinction, and grapple with the fact that she was often uncredited and barred from the scientific establishment as a poor woman. The lead approach is a story-and-perspective encounter in her voice; supporting approaches add a spatial/temporal anchor (cliff scene plus timeline), a re-enactment of fieldwork, and a light fact check. A recurring correction throughout: ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.

activities.title: Meet Mary Anning in her own voice
feedback: If a learner calls the finds dinosaurs, have Anning gently correct: 'No, those were sea reptiles — they swam in the ocean and are a separate group from dinosaurs.'
If a learner thinks fossil hunting was a safe hobby, have her describe the dangerous, crumbling cliffs (a cliff-fall killed her dog Tray) and that she sold fossils to feed her family.
If a learner assumes she was a trained, wealthy scientist, have her explain she was self-taught and largely outside the formal scientific world.
If a learner thinks she was always famous, have her explain that much of her work was published by men without naming her and that recognition came largely later.
Affirm answers that connect a named find (ichthyosaur or plesiosaur) to why it mattered: evidence that creatures once lived that no longer exist.
activities.rationale: Biography sticks when told as a story with a real person's obstacles — poverty, danger, being overlooked — and a first-person encounter lets children ask what she found, how it felt, and why she wasn't recognised, keeping both the science (extinction is real) and the injustice (who is remembered) central. A spoken, responsive exchange is well suited to carrying narrative and perspective; keep her answers within documented history and age-appropriate. This is a proposed design; comparative efficacy over other media is not established.
sourceClaims: Mary Anning (1799–1847) of Lyme Regis was a self-taught fossil collector who found the first correctly identified ichthyosaur (as a child, with her brother Joseph), the first complete plesiosaur (1823), and a British pterosaur; her finds were key evidence for extinction.

As a working-class woman, Anning was often not credited in scientific publications and was excluded from the Geological Society of London (which did not admit women at the time); wider recognition came largely after her death.
learnerActions: Picture standing on the windy shingle beach at Lyme Regis while Mary Anning works the cliffs, and ask her questions such as 'What did you find?', 'Was it dangerous?', and 'Why wasn't your name on the discoveries?'

Listen to her describe how her brother Joseph found a strange giant ichthyosaur skull (around 1811) and how she, as a girl of about 12, found and dug out the rest of the skeleton, and how she later uncovered the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton (1823)
Ask her why fossil hunting was risky and hear about working the crumbling sea cliffs and the landslides that endangered fossil hunters — one cliff-fall killed her dog Tray and nearly killed her

Ask her why her name was often missing from the discoveries and hear, plainly, that gentlemen bought her fossils and wrote scientific papers about them, often without naming her as the finder, and that as a woman she could not even join the Geological Society
Ask 'Were they dinosaurs?' and hear her correction that her famous beasts were sea reptiles, not dinosaurs
Retell, in your own words, one thing she found and one reason she matters
activities.intendedInsight: Mary Anning was a real person whose discoveries were key evidence that whole kinds of animals had gone extinct — a radical idea at the time — and whose lack of credit as a poor woman raises the question of who gets to do science and who gets remembered.

activities.title: Explore the Lyme Regis cliffs and a life timeline
feedback: When a find is revealed, confirm its name and that it is a marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
On the timeline, reinforce that she lived and worked in the early 1800s.
On the credit panel, affirm the honest point that recognition came largely later.
activities.rationale: A tappable cliff scene plus a timeline conveys place, era, finds and significance reliably and gives a spatial/temporal anchor. The linked reveals and comparison panels make the 'what changed' and 'why overlooked' threads concrete. On its own it does not deliver the first-person perspective, so it works well alongside or before the voiced encounter.
sourceClaims: Mary Anning (1799–1847) of Lyme Regis was a self-taught fossil collector who found the first correctly identified ichthyosaur (as a child, with her brother Joseph), the first complete plesiosaur (1823), and a British pterosaur; her finds were key evidence for extinction.

As a working-class woman, Anning was often not credited in scientific publications and was excluded from the Geological Society of London (which did not admit women at the time); wider recognition came largely after her death.
learnerActions: Tap features of a Lyme Regis cliff scene to reveal each labelled find — ichthyosaur and plesiosaur — and where along the coast she hunted
Tap points on a timeline of the early 1800s to reveal key life events and discoveries in order
Open a 'Why wasn't she credited?' panel to read, at an age-appropriate level, that her work was often published by men without naming her and that she could not join the Geological Society
Compare a 'credit then vs now' contrast: unnamed in old papers → celebrated today
Compare a 'before/after' on the idea of extinction to see what her fossils helped prove
activities.intendedInsight: The who/what/where of Anning's life — Lyme Regis, early 1800s, fossils in the sea cliffs — together with why her finds mattered and why she was overlooked.

activities.title: Prospect the Jurassic Coast like Anning
feedback: If a learner labels an uncovered specimen a dinosaur, correct: it is a sea reptile, a separate group.
Reinforce that real cliff hunting was dangerous and that Anning sold finds to survive, so it was work, not a safe hobby.
activities.rationale: Re-enacting the fieldwork engages children in what she did and makes the danger and skill tangible. Its limit is that it emphasises fossil-finding more than who she was and why she mattered, so pair it with the biographical encounter rather than using it alone.
sourceClaims: Mary Anning (1799–1847) of Lyme Regis was a self-taught fossil collector who found the first correctly identified ichthyosaur (as a child, with her brother Joseph), the first complete plesiosaur (1823), and a British pterosaur; her finds were key evidence for extinction.
learnerActions: Prospect a cliff scene safely to search for fossils where Anning worked
Uncover an ichthyosaur or plesiosaur specimen
Log and label the find as Anning did, noting that it is a marine reptile
Discuss what makes this hunting dangerous (crumbling cliffs, landslides)
activities.intendedInsight: A felt sense of what Anning actually did in the field — careful searching, uncovering, and identifying specimens — and that this was hazardous, hands-on work.

activities.title: Check the key facts and the big 'why'
feedback: Full understanding: names a discovery, explains her finds gave evidence for extinction and prehistoric life, AND distinguishes marine reptiles from dinosaurs.
Partial: names a discovery and says she was important but cannot say why, or still calls her finds dinosaurs — prompt for the 'why it mattered' and the reptile/dinosaur distinction.
Gap: recalls only 'found fossils' or 'found dinosaurs' — reteach using the story and the cliff/timeline.
If a learner says 'she just picked up pretty rocks; it wasn't real science,' connect her specimens to the scientific debates of the time: experts used them to understand extinction and ancient life.
If a learner assumes extinction was already accepted, set the context: the idea that whole kinds of creatures had vanished was new and contested, and her fossils helped establish it.
activities.rationale: A short check verifies the target facts and surfaces the common 'dinosaur' misconception and the 'just pretty rocks' undervaluing. A closed check assesses recall and can prompt brief explanation, but it does not itself convey the human story, so use it after the narrative work.
sourceClaims: Mary Anning (1799–1847) of Lyme Regis was a self-taught fossil collector who found the first correctly identified ichthyosaur (as a child, with her brother Joseph), the first complete plesiosaur (1823), and a British pterosaur; her finds were key evidence for extinction.

As a working-class woman, Anning was often not credited in scientific publications and was excluded from the Geological Society of London (which did not admit women at the time); wider recognition came largely after her death.
learnerActions: Match each find to its name (ichthyosaur, plesiosaur)
Answer why her work mattered and why she was often overlooked

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'Mary Anning dug up the skeleton of an ichthyosaur — a giant sea creature no one had ever seen alive. Why was a discovery like this so important for science? And does finding it make Mary Anning a dinosaur hunter?'
Explain in your own words whether ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were dinosaurs
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of place, era, a named find, and the significance (evidence for extinction and prehistoric life), while distinguishing marine reptiles from dinosaurs.

constraints: Keep all of Anning's voiced content within documented history and age-appropriate; address credit and gender honestly but gently for ages 7–9.
Treat the fieldwork re-enactment as a scaffold for 'what she did': it emphasises fossil-finding and must be paired with biographical content to convey who she was and why she matters.
Treat the fact-check as light assessment: recognition and short-answer items confirm recall and can prompt explanation but do not by themselves teach the human story.
Consistently correct the core misconception: ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs (links to real-vs-fiction and classification).
Present the pterosaur and coprolite work as additional context, not required recall for this age band; required evidence is place/era, one named find, and why her work mattered.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; the two cited claims are marked verified:false in the source and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed 3D as 'adds spectacle without teaching' and dialogue/quiz as unable to convey the human story; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims. They have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

The source recommendation that meeting her 'in her own voice' makes learning 'land in a way a caption never could' is a design claim, not evidenced; the comparative phrasing has been removed from the activity rationale, which now states only that comparative efficacy over other media is not established.
The 1823 date for the first complete plesiosaur and the 1799–1847 lifespan are taken from the source claims and not independently re-verified here.

probeDeeper: Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs lived in the sea and weren't dinosaurs — so why do we still study Mary Anning in a dinosaur topic?
What did her fossils help people realise about animals that lived long ago?
Why might it have been hard for a woman like Mary Anning to be taken seriously by scientists at the time?
assess.correctAnswer: Her fossils were evidence that creatures once lived that no longer exist anywhere — helping people accept that species can go extinct and that prehistoric life was different from today. But ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were marine reptiles, not dinosaurs, so she was a fossil hunter rather than strictly a dinosaur hunter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any big prehistoric reptile is a dinosaur: 'she was a dinosaur hunter who dug up dinosaurs.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-draw the boundary: ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were sea reptiles, a separate group from dinosaurs, however impressive.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — she was a famous dinosaur hunter who dug up dinosaurs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the ichthyosaur and plesiosaur as dinosaurs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Undervalues the work: 'she just picked up pretty rocks; it wasn't real science.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect her specimens to the scientific debates of the time — they were evidence experts used to understand extinction and ancient life.
errorPatterns.distractor: She just collected pretty rocks; it wasn't really science.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats her as a lucky collector with no scientific significance.

errorPatterns.pattern: Anachronism — extinction was already accepted, so it was no big deal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Set the historical context: the idea that whole kinds of creatures had vanished was new and contested; her fossils helped establish it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes people in the early 1800s already knew animals could go extinct.

responseLevels.gap: Recalls only that she 'found fossils' or 'found dinosaurs,' with no sense of why it mattered and no distinction from dinosaurs.
responseLevels.full: Names a discovery, explains that her finds gave evidence for extinction and prehistoric life, AND distinguishes marine reptiles from dinosaurs.
responseLevels.partial: Names a discovery and says she was important but cannot say why (extinction, prehistoric life), or still calls her finds dinosaurs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Mary Anning dug up the skeleton of an ichthyosaur — a giant sea creature no one had ever seen alive. Why was a discovery like this so important for science? And does finding it make Mary Anning a dinosaur hunter?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only knows the name says 'she was famous' or 'she found dinosaurs.' A child who understands explains her finds gave evidence for extinction and prehistoric life, and recognises that marine reptiles are not dinosaurs.
